message.content:
In Blackjack, the Ace is the most flexible card because it can count as **either 1 or 11**—whichever is more advantageous to the player’s hand. Here’s how it works:

| Situation | How the Ace is valued |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| **Starting hand** | If you’re dealt an Ace and another card, you can choose 1 or 11. Most players will pick 11 unless the other card is a 10‑value (10, J, Q, K), which would make a “blackjack” (21). |
| **Adding to a hand** | When you hit and receive an Ace, you can add 11 to your total if it keeps the hand ≤ 21. If adding 11 would bust, you automatically count the Ace as 1. |
| **Multiple Aces** | If you have more than one Ace, you can treat each as 1 or 11, but you’ll never count two Aces as 11 at the same time because that would bust (22). For example, two Aces can be 12 (11+1) or 2 (1+1). |
| **Splitting** | If you’re dealt two Aces, you can split them into two separate hands. In most casinos, after splitting Aces you receive only one additional card per hand and cannot hit again on those hands. |
| **Blackjack** | An Ace plus any 10‑value card (10, J, Q, K) is a natural blackjack, which usually pays 3:2. |

**Bottom line:**  
- **Ace = 11** if it keeps the hand ≤ 21.  
- **Ace = 1** if 11 would bust the hand.  

This flexibility is why Aces are so valuable in Blackjack—they give you the best chance to stay under 21 while still having a high total.
